name: Introduction to Communication
description: A foundational course introducing students to the nature, functions, and contexts of human communication from self-concept to public speaking and digital media.

modules.title: What is Communication
modules.objectives: Define communication and explain its core components; identify the levels of communication and why studying communication matters. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 1: What is Communication.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 1: What is Communication.
modules.practiceNote: Label the components of the communication process using a real-life example
modules.assignment: Analyze the provided fictional scenario: a student sends a brief group-chat message about a deadline, two classmates interpret it differently, and the project is submitted late. Submit: a 250-word analysis. Include: sender, receiver, channel, message, feedback, and at least two forms of noise; then rewrite the message and feedback loop to reduce ambiguity. Evaluation: correct use of the communication model, specific evidence from the scenario, and a practical revision.

modules.title: Types & Functions of Communication
modules.objectives: Distinguish among intrapersonal, interpersonal, small group, public, and mass communication; describe the social, instrumental, and identity functions of communication. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 2: Types & Functions of Communication.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 2: Types & Functions of Communication.
modules.practiceNote: Identify which type and function of communication best fits each given scenario
modules.assignment: Use five provided or invented school-safe scenarios rather than recording private interactions. Submit: a chart and a 200-word comparison. Include: the communication level, primary function, channel, intended audience, and one quoted or described clue for each classification. Evaluation: accurate classifications, clear evidence for each choice, and one supported pattern across the five cases.

modules.title: Self-Concept & Communication
modules.objectives: Explain how self-concept and self-esteem develop and influence communication behavior; apply the looking-glass self concept. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 3: Self-Concept & Communication.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 3: Self-Concept & Communication.
modules.practiceNote: Complete a self-concept inventory: list 10 words that describe how you see yourself
modules.assignment: Analyze a fictional vignette in which a student receives conflicting feedback from a coach, a teacher, and a peer. Submit: a 350-word case analysis. Include: two examples of reflected appraisal, one social comparison, one possible effect on communication behavior, and a supportive response that avoids stereotyping. Evaluation: accurate use of self-concept concepts, evidence from the vignette, and respectful reasoning. No personal disclosure is required.

modules.title: Verbal Messages
modules.objectives: Analyze how word choice, language style, and denotative versus connotative meaning affect communication outcomes. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 4: Verbal Messages.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 4: Verbal Messages.
modules.practiceNote: Rewrite five ambiguous sentences to increase clarity and reduce potential for misunderstanding
modules.assignment: Select a political speech, advertisement, or public announcement and analyze it in 350 words: identify examples of connotative language, euphemisms, and either inclusive or exclusive language. Explain how each specific word choice likely shapes the audience's perception of the message. Submit: a document, worksheet, slide, image, or link that shows the completed work. Include: drafts, annotations, quotations, analysis, or revised writing from the Verbal Messages module, plus a short explanation of how your work supports your answer. Evaluation: the teacher should be able to see the final product, the steps or evidence used, and one clear connection to the module objective.

modules.title: Nonverbal Messages
modules.objectives: Identify and categorize types of nonverbal communication; explain how nonverbal cues complement, contradict, and regulate verbal communication. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 5: Nonverbal Messages.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 5: Nonverbal Messages.
modules.video2Note: YouTube — Your Body Language May Shape Who You Are (TED Talk)
modules.practiceNote: Categorize 10 nonverbal behaviors observed in a photo or video as kinesics, proxemics, haptics, chronemics, or paralanguage
modules.assignment: Analyze five provided descriptions of nonverbal behavior in school, workplace, and online-meeting settings. Submit: a table and a 200-word conclusion. Include: the channel (facial expression, gesture, eye behavior, posture, touch, space, or vocalics), likely function, scenario evidence, and one contextual factor that could change the meaning of each cue. Evaluation: accurate categories, evidence-based reasoning, attention to context, and avoidance of claims that a cue has one universal meaning. No experiment on other people is required.

modules.title: Listening Skills
modules.objectives: Differentiate types of listening; apply active listening strategies to improve comprehension and relational quality in conversations. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 6: Listening Skills.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 6: Listening Skills.
modules.video2Note: YouTube — 5 Ways to Listen Better (TED Talk)
modules.practiceNote: Practice active listening using the HURIER model in a 5-minute partner conversation
modules.assignment: Use a provided fictional conversation transcript. Submit: an annotated copy and a 250-word reflection. Include: four marked listening barriers, four revised responses using paraphrasing, clarifying questions, or perception checks, and a brief explanation of why each revision is more effective. Evaluation: accurate identification of barriers, responses that preserve the speaker’s meaning, and clear links to active-listening principles. No private conversation log is required.

modules.title: Interpersonal Relationships
modules.objectives: Describe stages of relationship development and dissolution; explain how trust, commitment, and communication patterns shape interpersonal relationships. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 7: Interpersonal Relationships.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 7: Interpersonal Relationships.
modules.video2Note: YouTube — What Makes a Good Conversation (TED)
modules.practiceNote: Map a personal relationship using Knapp's Staircase Model of relationship development
modules.assignment: Apply Knapp’s Relationship Model to a provided fictional friendship or mentorship case. Submit: a 350-word analysis. Include: the current stage, two quoted or paraphrased communication events as evidence, an explanation of how those events changed the relationship, and one limitation of applying a stage model to real relationships. Evaluation: accurate stage evidence, careful reasoning, and recognition that relationships may not follow a fixed sequence. No personal relationship disclosure is required.

modules.title: Conflict in Communication
modules.objectives: Identify sources and styles of interpersonal conflict; apply constructive communication strategies to manage and resolve conflict. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Assigned reading for Module 8: Conflict in Communication.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video for Module 8: Conflict in Communication.
modules.practiceNote: Identify your dominant conflict style using the Thomas-Kilmann self-assessment
modules.assignment: Analyze a provided fictional conflict about a shared project deadline. Submit: a 400-word case response. Include: the conflict source, each party’s conflict style, two quoted lines that escalate the conflict, revised I-statements and listening responses, and a proposed agreement. Evaluation: accurate conflict concepts, specific textual evidence, and a workable de-escalation plan. No personal conflict disclosure is required.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is NOT a component of the basic communication process?
quizQuestions.answer: Profit motive
quizQuestions.explanation: The basic communication process consists of sender, message, encoding, channel, decoding, receiver, feedback, and noise. Profit motive is not a component.

quizQuestions.question: Communication competence refers to:
options: The ability to memorize communication theories
The ability to communicate effectively and appropriately in a given context
quizQuestions.answer: The ability to communicate effectively and appropriately in a given context
quizQuestions.explanation: Communication competence means knowing what communication behaviors are effective and appropriate for a given context and being able to perform them.

quizQuestions.question: In the communication process, noise is best defined as:
options: Anything that interferes with creating or interpreting a message
The channel selected by the sender
quizQuestions.answer: Anything that interferes with creating or interpreting a message
quizQuestions.explanation: Noise may be physical, psychological, semantic, or technical and can disrupt meaning at several points.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Define or explain: Studying communication is valuable because.
quizQuestions.answer: Studying communication helps people build stronger relationships, solve problems, and participate more effectively in school, work, and civic life.
quizQuestions.explanation: Communication study matters because it improves practical choices in relationships, teamwork, public speaking, and everyday problem solving.

quizQuestions.question: Which level of communication involves only one person engaged in internal thought and self-talk?
quizQuestions.answer: Intrapersonal communication
quizQuestions.explanation: Intrapersonal communication occurs within an individual — the internal dialogue and self-reflection that takes place in one's own mind.

quizQuestions.question: The instrumental function of communication refers to using communication to:
options: Achieve practical goals and get things done
quizQuestions.answer: Achieve practical goals and get things done
quizQuestions.explanation: The instrumental function of communication involves using messages to accomplish tasks, make requests, or achieve practical objectives.

quizQuestions.question: Mass communication is distinguished from other forms primarily by:
options: Reaching large, diverse audiences through technology
quizQuestions.answer: Reaching large, diverse audiences through technology
quizQuestions.explanation: Mass communication transmits messages to large, heterogeneous audiences through media technologies such as television, radio, newspapers, and the internet.

quizQuestions.question: A student asks a teammate to upload the final file before a deadline. Which communication function is primary?
quizQuestions.answer: Instrumental
quizQuestions.explanation: The message aims to complete a practical task, so its primary function is instrumental.

quizQuestions.question: Self-concept is best described as:
options: The overall mental image you hold of yourself
The social roles assigned to you by others
quizQuestions.answer: The overall mental image you hold of yourself
quizQuestions.explanation: Self-concept is the complex mental picture individuals hold of themselves, encompassing beliefs about their personality, abilities, values, and roles.

quizQuestions.question: According to Charles Cooley's 'looking-glass self,' we form our self-concept primarily through:
options: Comparing ourselves to idealized media figures
Imagining how others see and evaluate us
quizQuestions.answer: Imagining how others see and evaluate us
quizQuestions.explanation: Cooley's looking-glass self theory proposes that people develop self-concept by imagining others' perceptions and judgments of them — society becomes a mirror.

quizQuestions.question: In Self-Concept & Communication, Self-esteem refers to:
options: The number of roles you play in society
An evaluative judgment about your own worth
Your awareness of others' emotional states
quizQuestions.answer: An evaluative judgment about your own worth
quizQuestions.explanation: Self-esteem is the evaluative component of self-perception — how positively or negatively a person judges their own worth and competence.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Which of the following is most likely to damage a person's self-concept?
quizQuestions.answer: Repeated negative feedback from important others is most likely to damage a person's self-concept.
quizQuestions.explanation: Self-concept is shaped by reflected appraisals; repeated negative feedback from valued people can become part of how a person sees themself.

quizQuestions.question: Connotative meaning of a word refers to its:
options: Technical usage within a specialized field
quizQuestions.answer: Emotional and cultural associations
quizQuestions.explanation: Connotative meaning encompasses the emotional, cultural, and personal associations a word carries beyond its objective dictionary (denotative) definition.

quizQuestions.question: The word 'home' has a different meaning than 'house' primarily because of a difference in:
quizQuestions.answer: Connotative meaning
quizQuestions.explanation: 'Home' and 'house' share a similar denotative meaning (a dwelling) but 'home' carries warmer connotative associations of family, comfort, and belonging.

quizQuestions.question: Jargon is best described as:
options: Specialized vocabulary understood within a particular group or profession
Vague language used to conceal meaning
Overly formal language used to impress others
quizQuestions.answer: Specialized vocabulary understood within a particular group or profession
quizQuestions.explanation: Jargon is technical or specialized vocabulary used within a profession, field, or group that may be unclear to outsiders.

quizQuestions.question: Using 'sanitation engineer' instead of 'garbage collector' is an example of:
quizQuestions.answer: Euphemistic language
quizQuestions.explanation: Euphemisms substitute mild or indirect expressions for words considered unpleasant or blunt, such as calling garbage collectors 'sanitation engineers.'

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is an example of haptics?
options: Speaking more slowly to emphasize a point
Maintaining eye contact during a conversation
Moving closer to a friend during a personal conversation
quizQuestions.answer: A handshake when greeting someone
quizQuestions.explanation: Haptics is the study of communication through touch; a handshake is a common form of haptic communication that conveys greeting, respect, or agreement.

quizQuestions.question: When a nonverbal cue repeats the verbal message (e.g., saying 'Turn left' and pointing left), nonverbal behavior is functioning as a:
quizQuestions.answer: Repetition
quizQuestions.explanation: Repetition occurs when nonverbal behavior repeats the same message as the verbal content (pointing left while saying 'turn left').

quizQuestions.question: Choosing to sit farther away during a formal interview is an example of which nonverbal channel?
quizQuestions.answer: Proxemics
quizQuestions.explanation: Proxemics concerns how people use physical space and distance in communication.

quizQuestions.question: A speaker says “I am calm” while speaking rapidly with tense posture. The nonverbal cues primarily:
quizQuestions.answer: Contradict the words
quizQuestions.explanation: The vocal and bodily cues conflict with the literal message, creating contradiction.

quizQuestions.question: Empathic listening involves:
options: Evaluating the logic of the speaker's argument
Understanding and sharing in the speaker's emotional experience
Listening only for key facts and information
Pretending to pay attention while thinking about something else
quizQuestions.answer: Understanding and sharing in the speaker's emotional experience
quizQuestions.explanation: Empathic listening requires attempting to understand and emotionally connect with the speaker's perspective and feelings, not just processing informational content.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is a common listening barrier?
options: Maintaining eye contact with the speaker
Mentally preparing your response while the speaker talks
Paraphrasing what you heard to confirm understanding
Asking clarifying questions after the speaker finishes
quizQuestions.answer: Mentally preparing your response while the speaker talks
quizQuestions.explanation: Rehearsing your response while the speaker is still talking diverts cognitive resources from listening, making it a significant listening barrier.

quizQuestions.question: Open-ended questions in active listening are valuable because they:
options: Can be answered with a simple 'yes' or 'no'
Invite the speaker to elaborate and share more fully
Redirect the conversation to a new topic
Demonstrate that you already know the answer
quizQuestions.answer: Invite the speaker to elaborate and share more fully
quizQuestions.explanation: Open-ended questions (e.g., 'How did that make you feel?') invite expansive responses, encouraging the speaker to elaborate and feel genuinely heard.

quizQuestions.question: Which response best demonstrates paraphrasing?
options: “So the schedule change left you unsure which deadline applies—is that right?”
quizQuestions.answer: “So the schedule change left you unsure which deadline applies—is that right?”
quizQuestions.explanation: A paraphrase restates the speaker’s meaning and checks whether the listener understood it accurately.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Which of the following is not one of the steps in the hurier listening model?
quizQuestions.answer: Interrupting is not one of the HURIER listening steps. A strong response should use Listening Skills vocabulary, answer the full prompt, and include reasoning or evidence rather than a one-word reply.
quizQuestions.explanation: HURIER stands for Hearing, Understanding, Remembering, Interpreting, Evaluating, and Responding.

quizQuestions.question: According to Knapp's Staircase Model, the first stage of relationship development is:
quizQuestions.answer: Initiating
quizQuestions.explanation: Initiating is the first stage in Knapp's model, involving first impressions and initial contact (greeting, making oneself approachable and presentable).

quizQuestions.question: Trust is foundational to interpersonal relationships because it:
options: Makes deeper self-disclosure and vulnerability feel safe
Guarantees the other person will always agree with you
Is established instantly upon meeting someone
quizQuestions.answer: Makes deeper self-disclosure and vulnerability feel safe
quizQuestions.explanation: Trust creates a psychological safe space that enables partners to be vulnerable and engage in deeper self-disclosure, which is essential for relationship development.

quizQuestions.question: Why does trust often support deeper self-disclosure?
options: It reduces the perceived risk of sharing vulnerable information
quizQuestions.answer: It reduces the perceived risk of sharing vulnerable information
quizQuestions.explanation: Trust can make disclosure feel safer, although people still choose appropriate boundaries.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Define or explain: In the 'experimenting' stage of knapp's model, communicators primarily engage in.
quizQuestions.answer: In the experimenting stage, communicators use small talk and safe self-disclosure to discover shared interests.
quizQuestions.explanation: Experimenting is the stage where people test possible connection through low-risk topics and limited personal disclosure.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is a constructive conflict communication behavior?
options: Describing specific behavior and its impact using 'I' statements
quizQuestions.answer: Describing specific behavior and its impact using 'I' statements
quizQuestions.explanation: 'I' statements describe specific behaviors and their impact without blaming ('I feel frustrated when meetings start late' vs. 'You're always inconsiderate'), making them constructive conflict tools.

quizQuestions.question: Stonewalling in conflict communication refers to:
options: Calmly presenting your perspective without interruption
Withdrawing from interaction and refusing to engage
Firmly restating your position until the other person agrees
Seeking a third-party mediator to resolve the dispute
quizQuestions.answer: Withdrawing from interaction and refusing to engage
quizQuestions.explanation: Stonewalling involves shutting down emotionally and withdrawing from communication — giving the 'silent treatment' — which prevents conflict resolution.

quizQuestions.question: The competing conflict style is characterized by:
options: High concern for self and low concern for the other party
Equal concern for self and the other party
Low concern for self and high concern for the other party
Low concern for both self and the other party
quizQuestions.answer: High concern for self and low concern for the other party
quizQuestions.explanation: Competing involves high assertiveness and low cooperativeness — pursuing one's own goals at the expense of the other party's needs.

quizQuestions.question: Which conflict style combines high concern for one’s own needs with high concern for the other party’s needs?
quizQuestions.answer: Collaborating
quizQuestions.explanation: Collaborating seeks a solution that addresses important concerns of both parties.

questions.question: Which model of communication depicts communication as a one-way process from sender to receiver without feedback?
questions.answer: Linear model
questions.explanation: The linear model (e.g., Shannon-Weaver, Lasswell) depicts communication as a one-way transmission from sender to receiver with no feedback loop.

questions.question: The relational function of communication is primarily concerned with:
options: Building and maintaining social bonds and relationships
Persuading others to change their beliefs
questions.answer: Building and maintaining social bonds and relationships
questions.explanation: The relational function of communication involves using messages to establish, develop, and maintain interpersonal connections and social relationships.

questions.question: Self-concept is primarily shaped by:
options: Feedback from significant others and social comparisons
A single formative experience in early life
Academic test scores and external achievements
questions.answer: Feedback from significant others and social comparisons
questions.explanation: Self-concept develops through social interaction — feedback from parents, peers, teachers, and cultural messages — rather than any single source or biological determinism.

questions.question: Denotative meaning refers to a word’s:
options: A message with no sender, receiver, or feedback
A behavior that increases blame during conflict
A meaning based only on private emotional reaction
questions.answer: Literal or dictionary definition
questions.explanation: Denotation is the direct or dictionary meaning of a word; connotation is the feeling or association that the word may carry.

questions.question: When someone smiles while delivering bad news, the smile is functioning to ______ the verbal message.
questions.answer: Contradict
questions.explanation: When nonverbal cues conflict with the verbal message (smiling while saying bad news), the nonverbal behavior contradicts or sends a mixed message.

questions.question: Active listening requires which of the following?
options: Planning your response while the speaker is talking
Full concentration and engaged responding to the speaker
Agreeing with everything the speaker says
Interrupting to ask questions before the speaker finishes
questions.answer: Full concentration and engaged responding to the speaker
questions.explanation: Active listening involves giving the speaker your full attention, working to understand their meaning, and responding in ways that show comprehension and engagement.

questions.question: In Knapp's Staircase Model, the 'bonding' stage is characterized by:
questions.answer: Public commitment to the relationship, such as a formal partnership, close public identity, or recognized long-term bond.
questions.explanation: In Knapp's model, bonding makes a relationship publicly recognized through formal or symbolic commitment.

questions.question: Why can an I-statement be more constructive than a blaming you-statement during conflict?
options: They describe the speaker's feelings and needs without directly blaming the other person
It allows you to blame the other person without seeming accusatory
A message with no sender, receiver, or feedback
A behavior that increases blame during conflict
questions.answer: They describe the speaker's feelings and needs without directly blaming the other person
questions.explanation: An I-statement describes a specific behavior, the speaker’s response, and a need or request without assigning a global negative label to the other person.

questions.question: A construction drill makes it difficult to hear a classroom presentation. This is primarily which kind of communication problem?
questions.answer: Physical noise
questions.explanation: The external sound interferes with transmission and reception of the message, making it physical noise.

questions.question: Silently rehearsing what to say before asking a question is an example of which level of communication?
questions.answer: Intrapersonal
questions.explanation: Intrapersonal communication occurs within one person, including internal thought and self-talk.

questions.question: A student changes how they participate after repeated teacher and peer feedback. This most directly illustrates:
options: The denotative meaning of a word
questions.answer: Reflected appraisal shaping self-concept
questions.explanation: Reflected appraisal describes how perceived feedback from others can influence self-concept and later communication behavior.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes denotation from connotation?
options: Denotation is direct meaning; connotation is associated feeling or idea
Denotation is nonverbal; connotation is always spoken
Denotation changes by posture; connotation never changes
questions.answer: Denotation is direct meaning; connotation is associated feeling or idea
questions.explanation: Denotation refers to a word’s direct or dictionary meaning, while connotation includes learned emotional or cultural associations.

questions.question: A listener nods while another person speaks, helping manage turn-taking. The nod primarily performs which nonverbal function?
questions.answer: Regulating interaction
questions.explanation: Nonverbal cues such as nodding can regulate conversational flow by signaling attention or inviting the speaker to continue.

questions.question: Which behavior is a listening barrier?
options: Rehearsing a rebuttal while the speaker is still talking
questions.answer: Rehearsing a rebuttal while the speaker is still talking
questions.explanation: Mental rehearsal divides attention and can prevent the listener from accurately understanding the speaker’s full message.

questions.question: The 'looking-glass self' concept explains self-concept development through:
options: How we imagine others perceive and judge us
questions.answer: How we imagine others perceive and judge us
questions.explanation: Cooley's looking-glass self proposes that self-concept forms as we imagine others' views of us and internalize those imagined evaluations as self-perception.

questions.question: In the communication process, noise refers to:
options: Anything that interferes with encoding, transmitting, receiving, or interpreting a message
Only loud sounds that interrupt speech
A message with no sender, receiver, or feedback
A behavior that increases blame during conflict
questions.answer: Anything that interferes with encoding, transmitting, receiving, or interpreting a message
questions.explanation: Noise includes any physical, semantic, psychological, or technical interference that changes how a message is created, transmitted, received, or interpreted.

questions.question: The instrumental function of communication serves to:
options: Accomplish practical tasks and achieve tangible goals
questions.answer: Accomplish practical tasks and achieve tangible goals
questions.explanation: The instrumental function involves using communication to get things done — making requests, giving instructions, completing transactions, and achieving practical objectives.

questions.question: Proxemics is the study of how people use:
options: Tone and rate of voice in conversation
Physical space and distance in communication
Gesture and body movement to convey meaning
Time and timing as communicative resources
questions.answer: Physical space and distance in communication
questions.explanation: Proxemics (Hall) examines how physical distance — intimate, personal, social, and public zones — functions communicatively in different relationships and contexts.

questions.question: The primary difference between hearing and listening is:
options: Hearing involves both ears while listening uses only one
Hearing is a physical process while listening involves active attention and meaning-making
Listening is automatic while hearing requires effort
Hearing requires silence while listening can occur in noisy environments
questions.answer: Hearing is a physical process while listening involves active attention and meaning-making
questions.explanation: Hearing is the passive, physiological reception of sound; listening is the active, cognitive process of attending to and making sense of the sounds received.

questions.question: Which pattern most directly supports trust in an interpersonal relationship?
questions.answer: Consistent follow-through and honest clarification
questions.explanation: Trust grows when communication and behavior are reliable and misunderstandings are addressed openly and respectfully.

questions.question: Explain the difference between denotative and connotative meaning, using one word in a school-safe example.
questions.answer: A valid response states that denotation is the word’s direct or dictionary meaning, while connotation is the feeling or association the word carries, and shows both meanings in a specific example.
questions.explanation: The distinction explains why two accurate words can shape an audience differently.

questions.question: A message intended as a joke is read as insulting because the text channel removed tone and facial cues. Which concept best explains the breakdown?
questions.answer: Channel and noise
questions.explanation: A text channel carries fewer nonverbal cues, and semantic or psychological noise can change interpretation.

questions.question: The accommodating conflict style is characterized by:
options: High concern for self and low concern for others
Low concern for self and high concern for others
Equal concern for self and others
Low concern for both self and others
questions.answer: Low concern for self and high concern for others
questions.explanation: Accommodating involves setting aside one's own needs and concerns to satisfy the other party — low assertiveness but high cooperativeness.

questions.question: Which revision is the clearest I-statement?
options: I felt left out when the schedule changed without a message; can we agree on an update process?
questions.answer: I felt left out when the schedule changed without a message; can we agree on an update process?
questions.explanation: The revision describes a specific behavior and impact, then makes a concrete request without labeling the other person.

questions.question: When interpreting a crossed-arm posture, the most responsible conclusion is:
options: Context and clusters of cues are needed before inferring meaning
Body language reveals a person’s thoughts with certainty
The cue has the same meaning in every culture
questions.answer: Context and clusters of cues are needed before inferring meaning
questions.explanation: Nonverbal cues are ambiguous; setting, culture, baseline behavior, and other cues affect interpretation.

questions.question: Pseudo-conflict is best resolved by:
options: Allowing one party to win the argument
Clarifying the misunderstanding that created the apparent conflict
Seeking an external mediator to decide the outcome
Avoiding the topic that caused the perceived conflict
questions.answer: Clarifying the misunderstanding that created the apparent conflict
questions.explanation: Since pseudo-conflict is based on misperception or misunderstanding rather than real incompatibility, clarifying the misunderstanding typically dissolves the conflict.

questions.question: Which listener response is a perception check?
options: If I understood you, the changed deadline—not the task itself—is the concern. Is that right?
I already know what you mean.
questions.answer: If I understood you, the changed deadline—not the task itself—is the concern. Is that right?
questions.explanation: A perception check states a tentative interpretation and asks the speaker to confirm or correct it.

questions.question: A classmate says, “Fine, do whatever you want,” while looking away and speaking quietly. Explain two plausible interpretations and state what question could clarify the message.
questions.answer: A valid response recognizes that the words and nonverbal cues may conflict, offers two context-sensitive interpretations, and proposes a neutral clarification such as, “I may be reading mixed signals—are you comfortable with this plan?”
questions.explanation: Responsible interpretation avoids treating one nonverbal cue as proof and uses feedback to check meaning.

questions.question: Which response best demonstrates empathic listening?
options: Paraphrasing both the speaker’s concern and emotion, then checking accuracy
Planning a rebuttal while the speaker talks
questions.answer: Paraphrasing both the speaker’s concern and emotion, then checking accuracy
questions.explanation: Empathic listening attends to content and feeling while allowing the speaker to correct the listener’s interpretation.

questions.question: Why can clear boundaries support a trusting relationship?
options: They help people understand what information and behavior each person is comfortable with
questions.answer: They help people understand what information and behavior each person is comfortable with
questions.explanation: Clear boundaries support voluntary, appropriate disclosure and reduce uncertainty about expectations; trust does not require sharing everything.

questions.question: In Knapp’s model, experimenting is most associated with:
options: Small talk and low-risk disclosure to find common ground
questions.answer: Small talk and low-risk disclosure to find common ground
questions.explanation: Experimenting uses safe topics and limited disclosure to explore possible connection.

questions.question: Which behavior is most likely to escalate a conflict?
options: Using an absolute accusation such as “You always ruin everything”
questions.answer: Using an absolute accusation such as “You always ruin everything”
questions.explanation: Global blame and absolutes attack identity rather than address a specific behavior or need.

questions.question: Which response best uses collaborative conflict management?
options: Let us identify both priorities and test a plan that addresses each one.
We should avoid the issue indefinitely.
questions.answer: Let us identify both priorities and test a plan that addresses each one.
questions.explanation: Collaboration combines concern for one’s own needs with concern for the other party’s needs.

questions.question: Which of the following communication behaviors would best demonstrate active listening?
options: Looking at your phone while the speaker talks
Nodding, making eye contact, and paraphrasing what the speaker said
Immediately sharing your own related experience when the speaker pauses
Mentally preparing counterarguments while the speaker is talking
questions.answer: Nodding, making eye contact, and paraphrasing what the speaker said
questions.explanation: Active listening behaviors include attentive nonverbal signals (nodding, eye contact) and verbal feedback (paraphrasing) that demonstrate comprehension and genuine engagement.

questions.question: Rewrite this blaming message as a constructive conflict message: “You never do your part.” Include an observation, impact or feeling, and a specific request.
questions.answer: One valid response is: “The last two assigned sections were not uploaded by the agreed deadline, and I felt stressed because I could not assemble the final file. Can we assign owners and confirm uploads by 6 p.m.?”
questions.explanation: Constructive messages describe observable behavior, explain impact, and make a specific request without global labels.
